record.title: When a past opinion meets today

narrativeBridge.bridgeFromSource: Emerson questions whether yesterday's public opinion must govern the judgment you make with today's reasons.
narrativeBridge.situationHook: You publicly supported a neighborhood plan. New facts raise doubts, but neighbors expect you to stay consistent. Changing course might help—or might not.
narrativeBridge.playPrompt: Keep the plan, or open it to reconsideration?

record.intro: A neighborhood group must revisit a public plan. New details emerge, and everyone remembers what you previously said. The dilemma is whether consistency is serving the question or merely your reputation.
record.humanTension: Keeping a public promise of consistency or revisiting your judgment when circumstances shift.
record.sourceThesis: Fidelity to earlier words is not always faithful to present judgment
record.evidenceClaim: A mistaken insistence on consistency can inhibit independent thought
record.epistemicLimits: A revised view is not automatically wiser, nor is keeping a view always cowardly
record.compactLimit: Revision itself cannot guarantee a better judgment
record.counterexample: Emerson criticizes foolish consistency, not every principled commitment
record.readerAgency: Choose a stance before seeing an invented complication and reconsider
record.reflectionQuestion: When might a changed answer express integrity rather than mere inconsistency?
supportedConclusions: Past statements are not sufficient evidence for a present judgment
